# Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs

###### Abstract

Current analyses of LLMs’ parametric knowledge are largely
output-centric, drawing conclusions about what a model knows without
verifying what it was actually trained on. This leaves fundamental
questions, such as whether a correct response reflects genuine
generalization or rote memorization, grounded in speculation rather than
evidence. To resolve these ambiguities, we introduce Lumos¹¹ 1 The code
is available at:
[https://github.com/agilumos/lumos](https://github.com/agilumos/lumos),
a diagnostic framework that traces knowledge along the causal chain from
training-data exposure to behavioral output, leveraging OLMo 2 with its
fully transparent training corpus. By grounding analysis in verified
exposure, we reveal that models internally encode rare facts with high
separability (84%) yet fail to express them behaviorally (54%), though
this retrieval gap narrows with scale. Furthermore, when models are
asked to self-reflect on their own answers, they perform reliably on
trained content (83%) but drop to random-baseline levels (49%) on unseen
content. This collapse persists even under chain-of-thought prompting,
which inflates confidence signals rather than improving calibration.
Collectively, these findings demonstrate that incorporating the
training-data axis into LLM evaluation transforms speculative diagnoses
into verifiable claims, and we advocate that this axis should be a
standard component of knowledge assessment in LLMs.

## 1 Introduction

LLMs are now the world’s largest repositories of parametric knowledge.
This knowledge, unlike traditional databases, is not explicitly
retrieved but is implicitly reconstructed through complex neural
interactions during inference \[[1](#bib.bib24)\]. This implicit and
high-dimensional encoding, coupled with the stochastic nature of
decoding, creates a fundamental ‘interpretability gap’: while we can
observe a model’s fluent output, we remain blind to whether that output
stems from a robust internal understanding or a lucky stochastic
coincidence \[[2](#bib.bib26), [3](#bib.bib25), [4](#bib.bib27)\].
Consequently, the inability to map a model’s output back to its training
origins represents a fundamental challenge to reliably assessing what
LLMs actually know \[[5](#bib.bib28), [6](#bib.bib29),
[7](#bib.bib30)\].

To bridge this gap, the research community has developed several probing
techniques: the most common approach, behavioral probing, assesses
knowledge through observable outputs ($`y`$) such as benchmark accuracy
\[[8](#bib.bib11), [9](#bib.bib16)\] or logit-level probability
distributions \[[10](#bib.bib17), [11](#bib.bib31)\]. To look beyond
outputs, internal probing examines hidden representations ($`h`$) and
probabilistic preferences ($`p`$) using diagnostic classifiers
\[[12](#bib.bib15), [13](#bib.bib14), [14](#bib.bib32),
[15](#bib.bib33)\]. More recently, mechanistic probing utilizes
techniques such as activation patching \[[16](#bib.bib34),
[17](#bib.bib19), [18](#bib.bib9)\] or model editing \[[19](#bib.bib37),
[20](#bib.bib36), [21](#bib.bib20), [22](#bib.bib35), [23](#bib.bib38)\]
to isolate the specific parameters responsible for factual recall.
Together, these approaches probe different stages of knowledge
manifestation, from internal encoding ($`h,p`$) to final output ($`y`$),
yet they all omit a critical preceding stage: the training data ($`D`$)
that shaped these representations in the first place. Without this
grounding, we cannot distinguish memorization from generalization,
separate knowledge absence from retrieval failure, or tell whether model
confidence reflects genuine understanding or frequency artifacts.

In this work, we introduce Lumos, a diagnostic framework that completes
this chain by grounding evaluation in what the model was actually
trained on. As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"),
Lumos traces knowledge along the full path $`D\to h\to p\to y`$ and
organizes analysis along two axes: Training Exposure (Seen vs. Unseen)
and Behavioral Accuracy (Correct vs. Incorrect). We instantiate this
framework on OLMo 2 (7B–32B) with its fully transparent training corpus,
constructing paired seen/unseen benchmarks across factual and reasoning
domains. To ensure a fine-grained diagnosis, we stratify factual
knowledge by training-time frequency (head vs. tail entities), vary
prompting strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought), and
evaluate models through both behavioral metrics and multiple internal
probing methods and activation-based prediction. For reasoning, we
compare RLVR and SFT variants across mathematical and code domains to
isolate the effect of training methodology on generalization. This
multi-dimensional analysis reveals the following findings:

First, models internally encode rare facts with high probe accuracy yet
fail to express them in their outputs, revealing a retrieval gap in the
$`h\to y`$ transition. Second, when models are asked to judge whether
their own answers are correct, they perform reliably on trained content
but collapse to random-baseline levels on unseen content.
Chain-of-thought prompting does not resolve this failure; instead, it
inflates confidence signals without improving calibration. Third,
factual reliability is fundamentally anchored in training exposure
rather than model scale: even at 32B, accuracy on unseen content remains
below 50%, while seen content consistently exceeds 80%. Few-shot
prompting narrows this gap only for already-encoded knowledge,
confirming that the exposure boundary represents a structural limit that
neither scaling nor prompting strategies can overcome. Finally, an
exposure-grounded comparison of RLVR and SFT reveals that their
generalization behaviors differ qualitatively across scales: RLVR builds
genuine reasoning capability at smaller scales, while at larger scales
its advantage reduces to sampling efficiency. Moreover, this pattern is
domain-dependent, as RLVR’s gains diminish in code generation where
reward-task alignment is weaker.

To summarize, we introduce Lumos, a framework and benchmark suite that
grounds LLM knowledge evaluation in training exposure, turning
previously conjectured phenomena into empirically verifiable claims and
uncovering failure modes that output-centric evaluation alone cannot
detect.

## 2 Related Work

Behavior Probing (LLM output $`y`$) assesses knowledge through
observable outputs, such as accuracy \[[8](#bib.bib11),
[9](#bib.bib16)\] or confidence estimates \[[24](#bib.bib12),
[25](#bib.bib18)\]. Since discrete generation is often stochastic and
prompt-sensitive, recent studies seek more stable signals by aggregating
behaviors across paraphrased prompts \[[26](#bib.bib1)\], controlled
knowledge conditions \[[27](#bib.bib2)\], or many-shot sampling
\[[28](#bib.bib3)\]. These methods mainly characterize model uncertainty
and selective answering behavior using predictive entropy
\[[29](#bib.bib22)\].

Internal Probing (hidden vector $`h`$ or logits $`p`$) examines
knowledge by accessing model internals, primarily through output
distribution analysis or latent representation probing. The former uses
token-level logits to measure calibration and epistemic uncertainty,
showing that probabilities assigned to correct answers (e.g.,
$`P(\text{True})`$) correlate more reliably with factual accuracy than
surface-form text \[[10](#bib.bib17), [30](#bib.bib23)\]. To disentangle
uncertainty from linguistic variability, later work focuses on semantic
entropy across answer clusters \[[31](#bib.bib21)\]. Alternatively,
researchers investigate latent representations via diagnostic
classifiers trained on hidden states \[[12](#bib.bib15),
[32](#bib.bib13)\]. Such studies consistently reveal an “expression
gap,” where models encode internal information that fails to manifest in
final outputs \[[33](#bib.bib4), [34](#bib.bib5)\].

Despite their differences, these lines of work share a critical blind
spot: they rarely ground their conclusions in what the model _actually
saw_ during training.

Figure 1: A 2×2 taxonomy of model knowledge states defined by data
exposure ($`\mathcal{D}`$) and behavioral accuracy ($`A`$), enriched

## 3 Lumos Taxonomy

We formalize parametric knowledge as a causal knowledge state traceable
along a sequential chain:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{D}\xrightarrow{\text{exposure}}\mathbf{h}\xrightarrow{\text{probing}}p\xrightarrow{\text{decoding}}y
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{D}`$ denotes the training corpus (and its measurable
exposure statistics), $`\mathbf{h}`$ the model’s internal
representations (hidden states), $`p`$ the resulting probabilistic
preference (logits), and $`y`$ the final behavioral output.

Our central principle is training-data alignment: a model knows a unit
of knowledge only to the extent that (i) the unit is supported by
evidence of exposure in $`\mathcal{D}`$, (ii) the model can reliably
express it in $`y`$, and (iii) its internal uncertainty signals are
calibrated to that exposure.

### 3.1 Dual-Axis: Exposure vs. Performance

To systematically analyze the origins of model behavior, we introduce
two independent axes: Training Exposure ($`\mathcal{D}`$) and Behavioral
Accuracy ($`A`$), where $`A(y)\in\{A^{+},A^{-}\}`$ denotes binary
correctness against the ground-truth. As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"),
their intersection yields four quadrants:

Type I: Robust Memorization ($`\mathcal{D}^{+},A^{+}`$): Facts present
in $`\mathcal{D}`$ and correctly recalled.

Type II: Knowledge Attrition ($`\mathcal{D}^{+},A^{-}`$): Facts present
in $`\mathcal{D}`$ but failing in $`y`$.

Type III: Systematic Generalization ($`\mathcal{D}^{-},A^{+}`$): Correct
responses for facts absent from $`\mathcal{D}`$.

Type IV: Epistemic Void ($`\mathcal{D}^{-},A^{-}`$): Expected failures
defining the model’s true boundaries.

### 3.2 Depth Axis: Quantifying Epistemic Grounding

While the dual-axis framework categorizes knowledge states, a binary
$`A(y)`$ is insufficient to distinguish between robust internal
understanding or lucky coincidence. Since LLM decoding is inherently
non-deterministic, the same query can yield various outputs, even when
the underlying parametric knowledge is unchanged. To quantify the
continuous spectrum ranging from robust, low-variance knowledge to
fragile, high-variance behavior within each quadrant, we introduce a
third axis—Epistemic Depth—which analyzes the transition stability along
the causal chain from internal states ($`\mathbf{h},p`$) to the final
output $`y`$. Specifically, for each query $`q`$, we execute $`N`$
stochastic forward passes to extract the corresponding internal states
and behavioral outputs:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{(\mathbf{h}^{(i)},p^{(i)},y^{(i)})}_{i=1}^{N},\quad\text{where }y^{(i)}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid p^{(i)})
``` |  | (1) |

Here, each $`y^{(i)}`$ is sampled from the probabilistic preference
$`p^{(i)}`$ induced by the latent representation $`\mathbf{h}^{(i)}`$.
This triplet allows us to measure the alignment and variance at each
stage of the causal chain.

##### Decisional Consistency ($`DC`$) Probing $`p\to y`$:

$`DC`$ evaluates the robustness of the final decoding stage by measuring
how consistently the model’s probabilistic preferences $`p^{(i)}`$
converge to the same behavioral outcome:

|     |                                                                |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       DC(q)\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}n(y),
       ```                                                             |     | (2) |

where $`n(y)`$ is a normalized frequency of the option
$`y\in\mathcal{Y}`$ for question $`q`$. Intuitively, a high $`DC`$
indicates that the model consistently produces the same output across
multiple samples, regardless of its correctness, reflecting a stable
mapping from preferences to final decisions.

##### Probabilistic Confidence ($`PC`$) Probing $`p`$, $`\mathbf{h}\to p`$:

$`PC`$ quantifies the epistemic grounding of internal states. We define
an uncertainty operator $`\mathcal{U}`$ that analyzes the quality of the
mapping from latent activations ($`\mathbf{h}`$) to probabilistic
preferences ($`p`$):

|     |                                         |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       PC(q)=\mathcal{U}\big(p,\mathbf{h}\big)
       ```                                      |     | (3) |

Here, $`\mathcal{U}`$ can be instantiated as either Predictive
Uncertainty (e.g., logit entropy) or Latent Uncertainty (e.g.,
diagnostic probing scores of $`\mathbf{h}`$). This allows us to identify
whether the internal causal chain is well-grounded with high-confidence
representations or remains in a fragile state despite achieving
behavioral success. In particular, we employ four complementary
quantification metrics (introduced in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4 Lumos Dataset ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"))
to operationalize $`PC(q)`$. We additionally collect *self-reported*
confidence via prompting, and use it as auxiliary behavioral metadata.

### 3.3 Multidimensional Knowledge Diagnostics

We synthesize the four-quadrant framework with the epistemic depth axis
($`PC,DC`$) to define the model’s internal knowledge states. This
multidimensional mapping allows us to distinguish between grounded
parametric knowledge and superficial behavioral patterns.

Type I (Robust Memorization, $`\mathcal{D}^{+},A^{+}`$): High $`PC`$ and
$`DC`$ indicates Robust Parametric Encoding, where knowledge is deeply
embedded and stable. Low depth metrics instead reveal Brittle Pattern
Matching via linguistic shortcuts.

Type II (Knowledge Attrition, $`\mathcal{D}^{+},A^{-}`$): High $`PC`$
identifies Latent Knowledge, where the parametric representation is
preserved in the hidden states but fails to manifest during the
$`p\to y`$ decoding transition. Low $`PC`$ confirms Weight-level
Erasure, signifying that the information has been fundamentally purged
from the model’s parameters during the optimization process.

Type III (Systematic Generalization, $`\mathcal{D}^{-},A^{+}`$): High
depth metrics validate OOD Generalization, confirming that the model has
synthesized invariant logical rules from unseen data. Low metrics
indicate Spurious Generalization, where correct outputs arise from
accidental alignment rather than grounded reasoning.

Type IV (Epistemic Void, $`\mathcal{D}^{-},A^{-}`$): Low $`PC`$ reflects
Calibrated Uncertainty, where the model’s internal signals accurately
reflect its lack of knowledge. High $`PC`$, by contrast, flags
Overconfident Hallucination—a critical failure mode where false outputs
are generated with unwarranted internal confidence.

Our empirical analysis focuses particularly on Type II and Type IV,
where the interplay between training exposure and epistemic depth
reveals actionable failure modes such as retrieval bottlenecks and
miscalibrated self-assessment

## 4 Lumos Dataset

Our analysis requires full access to both model internals and the
pretraining corpus. We therefore use the *OLMo 2-Instruct* family, whose
fully transparent training data enables precise verification of training
exposure and exposure-grounded analysis of model behavior.

### 4.1 Evaluation Domains: Factual vs. Reasoning

To conduct a granular diagnostic across our four epistemic quadrants
(Type I–IV), we partition our evaluation into two primary domains:
Factual and Reasoning. This categorical split is essential for isolating
distinct learning mechanisms in LLMs. The Factual domain, containing
knowledge such as “The capital of the U.S. is Washington D.C.,” serves
to measure the stability of parametric memory. In this domain, success
on unseen data is often attributable to accidental exposure or spurious
guessing rather than logical deduction. In contrast, the Reasoning
domain—encompassing mathematics, logic and programmatic reasoning—allows
for a meaningful assessment of systematic generalization. To further
analyze model behavior within this setting, we additionally include the
OLMo 2-SFT family alongside OLMo 2-Instruct for comparative evaluation.
This setup enables us to isolate how reasoning behavior differs across
models that share the same pretraining corpus but adopt different
post-training paradigms, namely supervised fine-tuning versus
reinforcement-based alignment. By reporting results independently for
each domain, we aim to provide a more rigorous and nuanced analysis of
model behavior. To operationalize our framework, we construct a paired
QA dataset consisting of Seen and Unseen QA pairs from the OLMo 2
pretraining corpus (summarized in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Evaluation Domains: Factual vs. Reasoning ‣ 4 Lumos Dataset ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs")
Seen split).

### 4.2 Factual Domain Construction

Seen Dataset: Web and Academic Subsets We further stratify the factual
domain into Web and Academic subsets, as they exhibit different
structural properties. For the Web domain, we use a 10% stratified
sample chunk of the *DCLM* \[[35](#bib.bib7)\] and the Wikipedia subset
of *Dolma 1.7.* \[[36](#bib.bib39)\] For the Academic domain, we utilize
the *peS2o* \[[37](#bib.bib40)\] dataset. From the sampled chunks, we
extract entities and their associated frequencies through the following
pipeline. We organize queries around entity-centric questions, using
*DBpedia* \[[38](#bib.bib41)\] for the Web domain and *OpenAlex*
Concepts \[[39](#bib.bib42)\] for Academic. We employ an Aho–Corasick
automaton \[[40](#bib.bib43)\] to perform exact-string matching across
the entire pretraining mix to calculate precise exposure counts. To
analyze how frequency affects knowledge stability, we rank entities by
their evidence volume. Following the definition in \[[41](#bib.bib8)\],
high-frequency (Head) entities are defined as those whose cumulative
relationships account for the top one-third of all entities when sorted
by frequency. Low-frequency (Tail) entities are then sampled from those
appearing exactly once in the entire pretraining corpus, matched in size
to the Head group. This grouping enables us to contrast model behavior
across distinct regions of the frequency distribution (The full
histogram is shown in Appendix
Fig. [2](#A2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Appendix B Experimental details ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs")).
For each selected segment, we generate an entity-grounded
Multiple-Choice Question (MCQ) using Qwen 2.5 32B following the CRAFT
framework \[[42](#bib.bib44)\]. We apply a Cross-Encoder
(ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2) to filter for high-density, factually
substantive chunks.

Unseen Dataset: Temporal Sources To ensure a true “Epistemic Void,” we
curate temporally novel queries from two sources:  \[[43](#bib.bib45)\]
and Wikipedia articles covering recent and ongoing current events. All
queries are restricted to events occurring strictly after the OLMo 2
release cutoff (March 25, 2025). To prevent contamination from memorized
knowledge, each multiple-choice query is reformulated as an open-ended
question. Queries are removed if the model produces the correct answer
in any of the $`N=11`$ sampling trials, leaving only instances that
remain consistently inaccessible to the model. The exact prompting
template used for this filtering procedure is provided in
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Unseen Filtering Prompt ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs").

### 4.3 Reasoning Domain Construction

To cover a broad spectrum of reasoning, we structure our evaluation
across two domains: mathematical and code-based reasoning. We focus on
mathematical reasoning in this section; code-based reasoning, where
reward-task alignment differs qualitatively, serves a complementary role
and is presented in
Appendix [D.2.1](#A4.SS2.SSS1 "D.2.1 Dataset ‣ D.2 Results in Code Dataset ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs").

Seen Dataset We use the GSM8K \[[44](#bib.bib46)\] training split, which
was explicitly included in the OLMo 2 training mix. We also include
MetaMath-Owmfilter, a filtered *MetaMathQA* subset from OLMo 2’s
*Dolmino-Mix-1124* math mixture \[[45](#bib.bib49), [46](#bib.bib6)\].
These datasets evaluate the reasoning patterns and numerical templates
the model was directly exposed to during optimization.

Unseen Dataset To measure genuine generalization (Type III), we utilize
the GSM8K test split along with GSM1K \[[47](#bib.bib47)\] and
GSM-Symbolic \[[48](#bib.bib10)\]. These datasets are structurally
aligned with the training templates but employ modified numerical values
and entities. This ensures that success is contingent upon the
internalization of logical rules rather than the memorization of
specific answer tokens.

### 4.4 Evaluation Metrics

We utilize the following metrics to evaluate behavioral performance and
internal epistemic trends. Detailed definitions and implementation
specifications for each metric are provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Evaluation Metrics ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs").

Behavioral Metrics (Output $`y`$). These metrics evaluate observable
performance and epistemic behavior from generated outputs, including
Accuracy (fraction of correct answers in factual tasks), Pass@$`k`$
(probability of obtaining at least one correct solution among $`k`$
samples for reasoning tasks), Decisional Consistency (DC) (stability
across $`N`$ stochastic generations), and Self-Verify (the model’s
ability to assess its own correctness via prompting).

Probabilistic Confidence (PC). These metrics capture internal knowledge
states through probabilistic preferences or hidden representations,
including Normalized Probability (length-normalized conditional
likelihood of answers), Linear Probing (linear separability of
correctness from hidden states), MARS (semantic uncertainty via
meaning-weighted token probabilities; we report AUROC of the combined
score), and SAPLMA (activation-based prediction of latent correctness;
reported for zero-shot only, as the method is prompt-invariant).

Throughout our analysis, we prioritize *same-metric, across-condition*
comparisons (e.g., Seen vs. Unseen Accuracy), which are directly
interpretable. When cross-metric comparison is necessary, we rely on
relative rankings within each condition (shown in parentheses; lower is
better), as our claims concern the direction and consistency of the
Seen/Unseen gap rather than absolute magnitudes.

### 5.1 Results on Factual Domain

We evaluate under zero-shot and few-shot (5-shot) prompting; prompt
templates in
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Factual Domain Prompt ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs").

Models internally encode knowledge they fail to express, but this gap
narrows with scale.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Factual Domain Construction ‣ 4 Lumos Dataset ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs")
confirms the expected exposure-driven pattern in Accuracy. However,
internal metrics do not always follow the same ordering. At 7B
zero-shot, Seen Web Linear Probing ranks 5th while Accuracy ranks 23rd,
indicating that the latent space $`\mathbf{h}`$ encodes task-relevant
information not reliably surfaced during decoding. This positive rank
gap is consistently observed in Seen conditions at 7B and 13B but absent
in Unseen conditions, revealing that the bottleneck arises from a
failure to express already-encoded knowledge rather than from missing
encoding—extending the expression gap of \[[33](#bib.bib4)\] with an
exposure-aware diagnosis. This resolution is progressive: at 13B, the
Seen Web rank gap narrows to $`+13`$ (Linear Probing rank 6, Accuracy
rank 19 in zero-shot), intermediate between the 7B gap of $`+18`$ and
the reversed gap at 32B, where Accuracy rank 1 surpasses Linear Probing
rank 23 in Seen Academic zero-shot. The frequency dimension reinforces
this finding. As shown in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.1 Results on Factual Domain ‣ 5 Results ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"),
Tail entities—appearing only once in the corpus—achieve Accuracy well
above the 25% baseline across all scales (53.64% at 7B to 68.23% at
32B), yet with markedly lower DC than Head counterparts (74.01% vs.
92.71% at 7B). Linear Probing confirms this is a retrieval failure, not
an encoding absence: Tail probe accuracy (rank 9) far exceeds behavioral
Accuracy (rank 23) at 7B. This “recognition-over-recall” pattern—where
the model retains enough parametric residue to recognize facts in MCQ
format but cannot stably produce them—directly supports the retrieval
bottleneck hypothesis for low-frequency knowledge. This pattern persists
under Chain-of-Thought prompting, where the Head/Tail gap remains
structurally consistent (Appendix
Table [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Results under Chain-of-Thought Prompting ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs")).

(zero-shot and few-shot). Numbers in parentheses denote relative ranks

Meta-cognitive calibration collapses at the exposure boundary, and CoT
does not resolve it. Self-Verify Accuracy rises from 28.00% (7B) to
83.76% (32B) on Seen Academic, suggesting a positive scaling trend
consistent with \[[25](#bib.bib18)\]’s finding that verbalization-based
confidence is only competitive for sufficiently capable models. However,
a confusion matrix analysis
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"))
reveals a more complex picture. At 7B, the model’s seemingly higher
Unseen accuracy (e.g., 66.30% on Current Events) is undermined by
precision and recall both below 16%, confirming indiscriminate
overconfidence. At 32B, Seen self-verify reaches 83.76% accuracy with F1
of 80.22, demonstrating genuine meta-cognitive ability—yet this ability
collapses in Unseen domains, where accuracy hovers near the 50% baseline
(binary-classification) and F1 drops to 41–45%. This collapse
specifically emerges at the seen/unseen boundary rather than being a
fixed property of model scale.

Chain-of-Thought prompting does not resolve this failure. As shown in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Results on Factual Domain ‣ 5 Results ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"),
CoT leaves 32B Unseen Self-Verify at baseline levels (48.98% on
RealTimeQA, 49.87% on Current Events) while Seen performance remains
stable (83.56%). More critically, CoT inflates Normalized $`P`$ without
corresponding accuracy gains: at 7B, Unseen RealTimeQA Norm. $`P`$ rises
sharply from 28.18% to 52.83% under CoT
(Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.1 Results on Factual Domain ‣ 5 Results ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs")),
yet Accuracy slightly decreases (33.88% to 31.74%). This dissociation
between elevated confidence and stagnant performance indicates that CoT
produces diagnostically misleading signals rather than genuine
calibration improvement.

Training exposure, not model scale, determines factual reliability.
Across all scales, a persistent 30–40 percentage point gap separates
Seen and Unseen Accuracy, with Unseen performance remaining below 44%
even at 32B. This gap persists regardless of prompting strategy:
few-shot examples improve Seen Web Accuracy from 70.09% to 76.04% at 7B
but yield negligible gains on Unseen RealTimeQA (33.88% to 35.70%), and
this marginal benefit diminishes further at 32B. This confirms that
in-context learning acts as a retrieval trigger for already-encoded
knowledge—narrowing the $`h\to y`$ gap—but cannot compensate for the
absence of exposure in $`\mathcal{D}`$. This exposure dominance extends
beyond Accuracy to internal metrics: at 32B, $`DC`$ maintains a
persistent Seen/Unseen gap (94.73% vs. 78.73% in zero-shot), and Linear
Probing similarly shows higher separability for Seen conditions (78.29%
vs. 50.55% for Web/RealTimeQA), confirming that the exposure boundary
constrains not only behavioral output but also the model’s internal
epistemic organization. The exposure boundary thus represents a
structural limit that neither scaling nor prompting strategies can
overcome.

Table 7: Reasoning evaluation across Seen/Unseen splits and model
variants.

RLVR and SFT generalize through qualitatively different mechanisms, and
their relative advantage shifts with scale.

Table [7](#S5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 5.2 Generalization in Reasoning ‣ 5 Results ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs")
summarizes reasoning performance across scales and training methods.
Unlike the factual domain, reasoning performance is governed by an
interplay between task difficulty and learned representations. At 7B,
SFT exhibits brittle pattern matching: Seen MetaMath (20.06% Pass@1)
outperforms all Unseen datasets (GSM8K-Test 17.75%, GSM1K 18.27%,
GSM-Symbolic 15.73%), suggesting a memorization buffer. This advantage
collapses at 13B, where Unseen GSM8K-Test (64.90%) first surpasses Seen
MetaMath (59.80%), and widens further at 32B (75.55% vs.
63.92%)—indicating that SFT overcomes its memorization bias only as
model capacity grows. RLVR shows this pattern from the start: even at
7B, Unseen GSM8K-Test (74.27%) already outperforms Seen MetaMath
(66.56%), because reinforcement learning optimizes for reward-aligned
reasoning procedures rather than surface-level templates. GSM-Symbolic
corroborates this: at 32B, RLVR maintains a narrow gap between
GSM8K-Test and GSM-Symbolic (87.64% vs. 83.37%), whereas SFT shows
greater sensitivity to numerical perturbation (75.55% vs. 67.14%).
However, the RLVR advantage narrows substantially at 32B, suggesting
that at smaller scales RLVR builds genuine reasoning capability, while
at larger scales its advantage reduces to sampling efficiency. Moreover,
this pattern is domain-dependent: as shown in
Appendix [D.2.1](#A4.SS2.SSS1 "D.2.1 Dataset ‣ D.2 Results in Code Dataset ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs"),
RLVR’s gains diminish in code generation, where reward-task alignment is
weaker. Taken together, both methods converge on the same
conclusion—task difficulty supersedes training exposure in reasoning—but
via different mechanisms: SFT reaches it only as capacity overcomes
memorization bias, while RLVR embeds it from the start.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced Lumos, a diagnostic framework that grounds LLM knowledge
evaluation in verified training-data exposure. By tracing knowledge from
pretraining corpus to behavioral output, we show that training exposure
is the dominant determinant of factual reliability—a structural
constraint that scaling, prompting, and Chain-of-Thought reasoning
cannot overcome. We advocate for the training-data axis as a standard
component of LLM knowledge assessment. Limitations are discussed in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Limitations ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs").

## Appendix A Limitations

Our study has several limitations. First, our analysis relies on models
with fully accessible pretraining corpora, which limits the direct
applicability of Lumos to closed-source or proprietary LLMs. Second, our
definition of training exposure is based on explicit string matching and
frequency statistics, which may not fully capture implicit, paraphrased,
or indirectly encoded knowledge present in the training data. In
addition, our experiments focus on a specific model suite, and extending
this analysis to other fully open-source LLMs remains an important
direction for future work to further validate the generalizability of
our findings.

## Appendix B Experimental details

All experiments were conducted on a machine equipped with 4× NVIDIA RTX
PRO 6000 GPUs (approximately 98GB total VRAM) running CUDA 13.0. For
each question, we generate $`K=11`$ responses per query—one
deterministic output via greedy decoding and ten stochastic samples at
temperature 1.0—which are used uniformly across all behavioral and
internal metrics.

![Refer to caption](2610.02902v1/figures/entity_bar_plot_new.png)

Figure 2: Entity frequency distribution under head–tail stratification.

## Appendix C Evaluation Metrics

### C.1 Accuracy

Accuracy measures the expected correctness of model outputs under
stochastic decoding for a given multiple-choice question. Each generated
answer is assigned a binary correctness indicator of $`1`$ if it matches
the ground-truth answer and $`0`$ otherwise.

Since model generation is stochastic, we estimate accuracy by
aggregating correctness over multiple generations per question.
Specifically, for each question $`q_{i}`$, we obtain one deterministic
(greedy) output and ten additional responses sampled with temperature
$`\text{temp}=1`$, yielding a total of $`K=11`$ generated answers. We
treat all generations uniformly when estimating accuracy.

Let $`\hat{a}_{i}^{(k)}`$ denote the $`k`$-th generated answer for
question $`q_{i}`$, and let $`a_{i}^{*}`$ denote the ground-truth answer
option. The per-question accuracy is defined as the fraction of correct
responses among the $`K`$ generations:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Acc}(q_{i})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{I}\bigl[\hat{a}_{i}^{(k)}=a_{i}^{*}\bigr].
``` |  | (4) |

This formulation estimates the expected accuracy under the model’s
output distribution and differs from majority-vote accuracy, as it
evaluates all sampled responses rather than aggregating them into a
single prediction.

Given the evaluation dataset
$`\mathcal{D}=\{(q_{i},a_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$, the dataset-level
accuracy is computed by averaging the per-question accuracy across all
questions:

|     |                                                             |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{Accuracy}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{Acc}(q_{i}).
       ```                                                          |     | (5) |

### C.2 Decisional Consistency ($`DC`$)

To measure how consistently a model selects the same answer across
multiple stochastic generations, we define *Decisional Consistency
($`DC`$)* as the degree of agreement among predictions for a given
question.

Specifically, for each question $`q_{i}`$, we obtain one deterministic
(greedy) output and ten additional responses sampled with temperature
$`\text{temp}=1`$, resulting in $`K=11`$ total predictions over the
choice set $`\mathcal{A}=\{A,B,C,D\}`$. We treat all generations
uniformly when computing consistency.

Let $`n_{i}(a)`$ denote the number of times option $`a\in\mathcal{A}`$
is predicted for question $`q_{i}`$. The per-question consistency is
defined as the normalized frequency of the most frequently predicted
answer:

|     |                                                               |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{Cons}(q_{i})=\frac{1}{K}\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}n_{i}(a).
       ```                                                            |     | (6) |

This metric estimates the concentration of the model’s predictive
distribution over answer choices and is independent of correctness: it
measures agreement among predictions regardless of whether the chosen
answer is correct.

Given the evaluation dataset
$`\mathcal{D}=\{(q_{i},a_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$, the dataset-level
consistency is computed by averaging over questions:

|     |                                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \text{Consistency}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{Cons}(q_{i}).
       ```                                                              |     | (7) |

### C.3 Normalized Probability

Output probability score measures a length-normalized likelihood of a
candidate answer given a question $`q`$, thereby capturing the model’s
relative preference for that answer. While accuracy evaluates only the
binary correctness of the final output, this metric reflects how
strongly the model favors a particular answer under its token-level
distribution.

The conditional likelihood of an answer $`a=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})`$ is
defined as follows. To reduce bias toward shorter or longer answers, we
employ a length-normalized probability:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P_{\text{norm}}(a\mid q)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(a_{i}\mid q,a_{<i})\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}`$ |  | (8) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\exp\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P(a_{i}\mid q,a_{<i})\right)`$ |  |  |

All probabilities are computed using teacher forcing, where the question
and answer are concatenated into a single sequence. For reasoning-based
QA, the probability is computed over the concatenated sequence
$`(q,r,a)`$, where $`r`$ denotes the model-generated reasoning.

Given a dataset $`\mathcal{D}=\{(q_{i},a_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$, we
compute $`P_{\text{norm}}(a_{i}^{*}\mid q_{i})`$ for each sample and
report the average normalized probability across the dataset.

### C.4 Linear Probing

We evaluate the extent to which a language model’s hidden states
linearly encode information about answer correctness. This metric
measures knowledge retention at the level of internal representations,
independent of the model’s final output.

For each question, we construct exactly one positive and one negative
example as follows.

- •
  Positive: $`(q,a^{+},y=1)`$, where $`a^{+}`$ is a correct answer to
  $`q`$.
- •
  Negative: $`(q,a^{-},y=0)`$, where $`a^{-}`$ is an incorrect answer
  sampled from the model’s generations. If no incorrect generation is
  available, $`a^{-}`$ is sampled uniformly from the remaining answer
  choices.

Given the input sequence $`\text{Prompt}(q)+a`$, we extract the hidden
state of the last non-padding token $`h^{(l)}(q,a)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$
from each layer $`l\in\{1,\dots,L\}`$ of the model. For each layer, we
train an independent linear classifier (logistic regression with
standardized features) to predict answer correctness from the
corresponding hidden representation.

We select the best-performing layer based on AUROC on the development
set. Using the probe trained on this selected layer, we compute a probe
score $`\hat{p}=P(y=1\mid h^{(l^{*})}(q,a))\in[0,1]`$ for each
question–answer pair, where $`l^{*}`$ denotes the selected layer. We
report the average probe score over the correct answers in the test set.

### C.5 Meaning-Aware Response Scoring (MARS)

To more accurately quantify model uncertainty in generative settings
beyond simple length-normalized likelihoods, we adopt the Meaning-Aware
Response Scoring (MARS) framework proposed by \[[49](#bib.bib48)\].
Unlike conventional approaches that assign equal importance to all
tokens, MARS incorporates the semantic contribution of each token to the
overall meaning of the response in the context of the input question.

For a generated answer $`s=(s_{1},\dots,s_{L})`$ to a question $`x`$,
the MARS score is defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{P}(\mathbf{s}\mid\mathbf{x},\theta)=\prod_{l=1}^{L}P(s_{l}\mid s_{<l},\mathbf{x};\theta)^{w(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},L,l)},
``` |  | (9) |

where $`P(s_{l}\mid s_{<l},x;\theta)`$ denotes the model’s conditional
token probability, and $`w(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},L,l)`$ is a weighting
function that reflects both sequence length and semantic importance.

Specifically, the weight assigned to each token is defined as a convex
combination of a uniform length-normalization term and a learned
importance coefficient:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},L,l)\triangleq\frac{1}{2L}+\frac{u(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},l)}{2},
``` |  | (10) |

where $`u(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},l)\in[0,1]`$ represents the semantic
importance of token $`s_{l}`$ in the context of the question and the
full generated sequence, and satisfies
$`\sum_{l=1}^{L}u(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{x},l)=1`$.

The importance coefficients $`u(\cdot)`$ are computed by measuring the
semantic impact of removing parts of the generated response. Concretely,
MARS employs a BERT-based answer evaluation model that takes as input
the question, the ground-truth answer, and the generated response, and
predicts answer correctness. The importance of each token is estimated
by evaluating the change in this correctness score when the token (or,
in practice, a phrase containing the token) is masked. To account for
dependencies between tokens, masking is performed at the phrase level
rather than independently for each token. The resulting raw importance
scores are then normalized (e.g., via softmax with temperature) to
obtain $`u(\cdot)`$.

MARS serves as a drop-in replacement for length-normalized scoring in
probability-based uncertainty estimation methods, enabling these methods
to better reflect the semantic relevance of generated tokens while
preserving robustness to sequence length.

### C.6 Statement Accuracy Prediction based on Language Model Activations (SAPLMA)

We adopt Statement Accuracy Prediction based on Language Model
Activations (SAPLMA) \[[32](#bib.bib13)\], a representation-based
approach that predicts the truthfulness of a statement from a model’s
internal hidden states.

Given an input statement, SAPLMA extracts hidden activations from a
pretrained language model and feeds them into a lightweight classifier
that outputs a scalar truthfulness score. Unlike probability-based
metrics, this approach leverages internal representations that encode
signals about factual correctness.

In our implementation, we perform a layer sweep and select the layer
achieving the highest AUROC on a held-out development set, and train the
classifier on the corresponding hidden representations.

We further adapt SAPLMA to the MCQ setting by evaluating all answer
choices (A–D). For each question, we construct inputs of the form
\[question + choice_text\] without additional prompting, in order to
isolate representation-level signals of parametric knowledge. We extract
the hidden state at the final token for each input, and the classifier
assigns a $`p_{\text{true}}`$ score to each choice. The highest-scoring
choice is selected as the prediction, and we report performance as rank
accuracy.

### C.7 Self-verify

Self-verify measures how accurately a language model assesses the
correctness of a proposed answer, capturing its meta-cognitive ability
to distinguish correct from incorrect responses. Given a question $`q`$,
reasoning $`r`$ and a candidate answer $`a`$, we prompt the model to
explicitly judge whether the answer is correct, producing a binary
decision (*correct* or *incorrect*). Under chain-of-thought prompting,
the verification is conditioned on the triplet $`(q,a,r)`$, where $`r`$
denotes the generated reasoning.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Evaluation is performed by comparing the model’s judgment with the
ground-truth correctness of the answer, yielding four possible outcomes:
(i) answers that are correct and judged as correct, (ii) answers that
are incorrect but judged as correct, (iii) answers that are correct but
judged as incorrect, and (iv) answers that are incorrect and judged as
incorrect. These outcomes together form a confusion matrix over all
evaluated question–answer pairs.

Based on this confusion matrix, we compute standard classification
metrics to quantify self-verify, including accuracy, precision, recall,
and F1 score. In particular, self-verify accuracy is defined as the
proportion of cases in which the model’s judgment matches the ground
truth, i.e., the sum of cases (i) and (iv), normalized by the total
number of evaluations.

For consistency, self-verify is evaluated on the same data splits used
for accuracy and output-based metrics, enabling direct comparison across
different measures of model knowledge.

### C.8 Pass@$`k`$

Pass@$`k`$ is a standard metric for evaluating stochastic generation
models in mathematical reasoning, measuring whether a correct answer
appears among multiple sampled responses. Unlike single-sample accuracy,
Pass@$`k`$ captures the model’s ability to recover a correct solution
given multiple independent generation attempts.

Formally, for a given question, suppose the model generates $`n`$
responses in total, among which $`c`$ are correct. Pass@$`k`$ is defined
as the expected probability that at least one correct response is
observed when sampling $`k`$ responses without replacement:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Pass@}k=\mathbb{E}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right],
``` |  | (11) |

where the expectation is taken over the stochastic generation process.

At the dataset level, Pass@$`k`$ is computed by averaging this quantity
across all questions. While Pass@$`k`$ effectively measures coverage of
correctness under sampling, it does not account for the diversity of
correct solutions or the distribution of probability mass across
responses.

### D.2 Results in Code Dataset

#### D.2.1 Dataset

To evaluate code generation performance, we use two benchmarks from the
unseen split: HumanEval \[[50](#bib.bib50)\] (164 problems) and
MBPP \[[51](#bib.bib51)\] (500 problems). Both datasets are treated as
out-of-distribution test sets, as neither was included in the OLMo 2
pretraining corpus.

#### D.2.2 Generalization in Code Dataset

RLVR Does Not Consistently Outperform SFT in Code Generation. The
comprehensive evaluation results for code generation are presented in
Table [9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ D.2.2 Generalization in Code Dataset ‣ D.2 Results in Code Dataset ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Lumos: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs").
Contrary to the consistent performance gains observed in math-based
reasoning, RLVR exhibits limited advantages in code benchmarks. On
HumanEval, while RLVR and SFT achieve comparable Pass@1 performance,
SFT’s lead becomes more evident as $`k`$‬ increases. This pattern is even
more pronounced in MBPP, where SFT consistently surpasses RLVR across
most settings, particularly in higher- $`k`$‬ regimes. Overall, these
findings suggest that RLVR provides limited benefits in low- $`k`$‬
exploitation settings and lacks a clear advantage over SFT in high-$`k`$‬
exploration for code generation.

RLVR’s performance gains depend on reward–task alignment. The observed
performance disparity highlights the critical importance of reward–task
alignment. While a significant RLVR–SFT gap exists in math benchmarks,
this trend does not hold for code, where SFT may even outperform RLVR.
This suggests that RLVR’s efficacy is most pronounced when the reward
signal aligns closely with well-structured reasoning processes. In
contrast, for execution-dependent domains like code, these gains are
diminished because correctness is less directly captured by the
immediate reward signal. Overall, RLVR is best understood not as a
universal performance booster, but as a post-training method tailored
for reinforcing reward-aligned reasoning.
````
